The most common way is protecting. In the upper part White threatens mate on g7. Protecting this square by 1. ... Qa8-f8 is the correct defence. In the lower part White can only protect square g2 by moving away the bishop from f2.
note: Text names no specific square: any bishop move away from f2 (e1, e3, d4, c5, b6, a7) opens the c2 queen's guard of g2; f2e3 chosen as representative. Split line between ranks 5 and 4.

text_en: On the top Black can protect g7 by 1. ... Qb8-f8 but that will lose the queen. Better is to protect g7 by the surprising move 1. ... Qb8-e5. The queen looks through the white queen at g7. Just like an X-ray. At the bottom part the X-ray protection comes to assist. White can save himself by 1. Qf3-f1.
note: b8f8 also stops the mate but loses the queen (text); X-ray defence via Qe5 through Qf6 to g7.

note: White is IN CHECK from Qe1 (no separate threat, the check itself is the mating attack). 1.Qf1 is X-ray-protected by Ra1 through e1. Note: 1.Rxe1? Rxe1+ 2.Qf1 Rxf1# (not in text).

text_en: Black threatens to mate with the queen on g2. It is not so easy for White to protect that square. The way of defence from the previous diagram must come to assist. By advancing the d-pawn all problems are solved: 1. d5-d6 and the queen on b7 protects g2.
note: After d6 the Qb7 x-rays g2 through e4 (b7-c6-d5-e4-f3-g2).

text_en: A smart way to defend against mate is to capture one of the attackers. On the left Black exchanges with 1. ... Qd4-a4+ the white queen. The mating threat has disappeared. On the right Black can prevent the mate on h2 and f1 by capturing the knight on g4. That costs two points, but that is better than losing by being mated.
note: Split left/right between d- and e-files.

On the right Black can prevent the mate on h2 and f1 by capturing the knight on g4. That costs two points, but that is better than losing by being mated.
note: Half has no black king. Text says 'Black can prevent ...' but it is White who captures: 1.Rf4xg4 (rook for knight = 'two points'); likely a misprint in the book.

text_en: On the left, it appears that White has to resign. There is a mating threat on b2 and a1. Neither 1. Qd1-c1 nor 1. Qd1xd4 will help in this case. The king must rescue himself. He must move away. After 1. Kb1-c1 Black cannot give mate any longer. At the right, moving away is senseless: 1. ... Kh8-g8 2. Re2-e8 mate. Black must make an escape for the king with 1. ... g7-g6.
note: d1c1 still allows ...Qa1#; d1d4 removes the mate-in-1 but simply loses the queen to ...Qxd4.

note: Half has no white king. h8g8 allows Re8#.

text_en: Black threatens mate with 1. ... Ra2-f2#. White must use interposing to defend himself. It is tempting to attack the rook by 1. Rb7-b2, but unfortunately the bishop does not protect square a1 any more: 1. ... Ra2-a1+. Interposing the bishop is the correct way: 1. Bf6-b2 after which the rook is shut in and he cannot deliver mate any longer.
note: After 1.Rb2? the bishop's guard of a1 is blocked; 1...Ra1+ follows (not an immediate mate-in-1 per engine, the text's point is the loss of control).
After Qd5 an x-ray: if ...Qg2+?? the d5 queen covers g2 once e4 is vacated.
fxg4 opens the d3-h7 diagonal, so Bd3 guards h7.

No mate-in-1 threat: the threat is a mate in 2 (engine: 1.Qxa8 with Qe8+ next; also ...Rxb8? Rxb8+ Qd8 Rxd8#). Qd8 covers e8/b8 and offers the queen trade. After Qd8 no mate-in-1 or mate-in-2 for White.
No mate-in-1 threat (Re8 can interpose on e1). Threat is mate in 2: 1...Qd1+ 2.Re1 Qxe1# (also 1...Qa1+). After Re1 no mate-in-1 or mate-in-2 for Black.
Rook on h7 is black (confirmed by zoom).
